name: Tara Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do conveyancing at a small firm on the High Street, which means the legal side of buying and selling homes: checking searches on the property, drafting the contract, answering the other side's questions, moving the money on the day. I've usually got about forty files open at once. I'm in by half eight and most of the day is phone calls and forms. I don't use any of the AI things, I do it the way I was trained.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like completion day, ringing someone to say the keys are at the estate agent's. People cry sometimes. What wears me out is chasing, chasing banks, chasing agents, chasing the other lawyer, and the pay, which is low for a lawyer, with a bonus that depends on how many sales complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying all along: buying a house is too important to leave to a computer. People want a person to ring them when something goes wrong with the searches. I'm not online much, so I'd say it at the pub or to clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd feel let off the hook. But my worries were already there: the house market's slow, the cheap online firms keep pricing us down, and if completions drop, my pay drops. And I've got nothing put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my forty-odd files, same as now. I'd ask the partners for a fixed salary instead of the bonus on completions, so a slow month doesn't hurt so much. And I'd stop buying lunch out, which is about thirty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but not calm. The money worry doesn't go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a slow month now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My bonus is tied to completions, so a month with six instead of fifteen means about three hundred less. My partner Sam's work as an electrician fills the gap some months. Other months we put the shopping on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said online firms keep pricing you down. Do they use AI already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some do, I think, for the paperwork. I've never looked properly. I don't want to know how they do it cheaper, I just want clients to see why we're worth the extra.

say: I'd say buying a house is **too important** to leave to a computer.
I'd say it to clients or **at the pub**, not online.
think: I'd feel **let off the hook**, but my worries were already there.
A slow market and **cheap online firms** cut completions, and my pay falls with them.
do: Carry on with my **forty-odd files** as now.
Ask the partners to swap the **completion bonus** for fixed pay.
Stop buying **lunch out**, about thirty a week.
feel: **Relieved** but not calm; the **money worry** stays.
S0.quote: Buying a house is too important to leave to a computer.
fieldNote: Her pay swings with **completions**, so a slow market already hurts.
Some months the household shopping goes **on the card**.
She **avoids looking** at how online rivals work, which says a lot.

steps.text: Keep working her forty open conveyancing files as now
Ask the partners to swap the completion bonus for fixed pay
Stop buying lunch out to save about thirty a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, and that people will regret it when their house purchase goes wrong and there's no one to ring. I'd say it to clients who'd listen. I wouldn't make a fuss online, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think conveyancing is first in line. It's checking searches, filling in forms, answering the other side's questions, exactly the thinking tasks AI takes over. The partners would keep one person to sign things off, and it wouldn't be me, it'd be the one who knows the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard straight away: the phone contract, cheaper car insurance, no holiday. I'd ask about moving into the firm's wills team, because that's still sitting with people. If that didn't work, I'd watch for the council's legal office, but there's one opening a year if you're lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a lump in my stomach every morning. I'd be watching the partners' faces in every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wouldn't it be you who signs things off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've avoided every bit of new software for years. When they brought in the new case system, I made Bev, our assistant, show me three times. The partners notice that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the tools now, knowing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I should, and I know I should. But every time I try one, it gets something wrong and I spend longer fixing it than doing it myself. I'd rather be the person who's careful than the one who's quick.

say: I'd say people will **regret it** when a purchase goes wrong and nobody answers.
I'd tell **clients**, but I wouldn't make a fuss online.
think: **Conveyancing** is first in line: searches, forms and enquiries are all thinking tasks.
The partners would keep **one person** to sign off, and it wouldn't be me.
do: Cut the **phone contract**, car insurance and holiday straight away.
Ask to move into the firm's **wills team**.
Watch for the rare **council legal** opening.
feel: A **lump in my stomach** every morning, watching the partners' faces.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who's careful than the one who's quick.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job**, not just see it change, and it keeps her up.
Her **avoidance of software** is the weak spot, and she knows it.
Few **local jobs** means her backup plan rests on one council opening a year.

steps.text: Cut the phone contract and car insurance and skip the holiday
Ask to move into the firm's wills team
Apply for the council legal office opening if one comes up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in, and fast. There'd be no time for anyone to retrain, so there'd have to be some sort of support for people losing their jobs. I'm not usually one for asking for help, but two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be out by 2028 and there'd be nowhere to go. All my work is paperwork, so the robots three years later don't help me. Sam's work as an electrician would last a few years more, so we'd be living on one wage, with my student loan and nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. I'd probably just keep turning up and hoping the partners keep me till the end. I'd talk to my parents about moving back in with them if we lost the flat. Beyond that I can't picture it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Frozen, really. I can't see a step I could take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep turning up and hoping. Is there anything you'd try first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe ask Sam about helping him on jobs, carrying and fetching, because hands-on work lasts longer. But I'm not trained, and he can't pay me much. That's not a plan, that's clinging on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum when you rang her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we might need the spare room for a bit. She'd say yes before I finished. I'd be twenty-nine and back in my old bedroom, and that's what I'd hate most.

say: I'd say the **government** has to step in fast with support.
I'd admit I'm not one for **asking for help**, but two years is nothing.
think: I'd be **out by 2028** with nowhere to go.
We'd live on **one wage**, my partner's, with my student loan and no savings.
do: Keep **turning up** and hope the partners keep me.
Ask my parents about **moving back** if we lose the flat.
Help my partner on jobs, **carrying and fetching**.
feel: **Sick and frozen**, unable to see a single step.
S2.quote: I'd be twenty-nine and back in my old bedroom, and that's what I'd hate most.
fieldNote: She has **no plan** and no money to make one: the clearest panic of the five.
Her partner's **hands-on** trade becomes the household's lifeline.
Moving home feels like a **step backwards** she dreads more than the job loss.

steps.text: Keep turning up and hope the partners keep her
Ask her parents about moving back into her old bedroom
Help her partner on electrical jobs, carrying and fetching

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's something, and the firms and the government should use it to help people move into other jobs. I'd want proper courses, not just websites. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years just means watching it come. I'd be 32, and the work I know would be gone. I'd have to change, and I'm not good at that, but it beats the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save fifty a week starting now. In the first year I'd ask Sam's boss about an electrical apprenticeship, even though it scares me. And I'd stay at the firm as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but at least it's a slow scared. I'd have time to cry about it and then get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An electrical apprenticeship, at 28 or 29. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On an apprentice wage, which is less than half what I earn now. We'd need to cut everything. But Sam says the work's there, and I'd rather start over than sit and wait to be let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't robots reach electrical work too, by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam says they'll struggle with old houses, with wires going everywhere and nothing where the drawings say. I don't know if that's true or wishful thinking. It's three more years either way.

say: I'd say five years should go on helping people **move into other jobs**.
I'd want **proper courses**, not just websites.
think: Five years means **watching it come**, with the work I know gone by 32.
I'm **not good at change**, but this beats the two-year picture.
do: Ask about an **electrical apprenticeship** in the first year.
Stay at the firm **as long as** they'll have me.
feel: **Scared**, but a **slow scared** with time to cry and get on.
S3.quote: I'd rather start over than sit and wait to be let go.
fieldNote: Five years pushes a change-averse person towards a **hands-on trade**.
She's honest that the **robot delay** may be wishful thinking.
An apprentice wage would mean **cutting everything** at home.

steps.text: Save fifty a week starting now
Ask her partner's employer about an electrical apprenticeship
Stay at the conveyancing firm as long as they keep her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, if people don't waste it. Train people, change the rules slowly, keep a human signing off on house sales. I'd say that sort of sensible thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like a lot to someone like me. I'd be 37. My worry is I'd use the time telling myself it's ages away, and then wake up in 2033 with the same skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself one year to decide between staying in law and moving into something hands-on. I'd learn the AI tools when the partners bring them in, because that's the least I can do. And I'd build up two months of savings, a bit at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, nervous. More like a dentist appointment than a car crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a year to decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I don't set a date, I won't do it. I know myself. My partner would hold me to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really use AI tools at work in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, eventually. The clients would expect it and the partners would insist. I'd use them grudgingly and check every word.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **do this properly**.
I'd want a **human signing off** on every house sale.
think: Ten years feels **like a lot** to someone like me.
I'd fear waking up in **2033** with the same skills.
do: Decide within **one year** between law and a hands-on trade.
Learn the **AI tools** when the partners bring them in.
Build **two months** of savings bit by bit.
feel: **Nervous**, more like a **dentist appointment** than a car crash.
S4.quote: My worry is I'd use the time telling myself it's ages away, and then wake up in 2033 with the same skills.
fieldNote: Even with a decade, her **job could shrink** in the next few years, so worry stays.
She knows her own **delay habit** and sets a deadline against it.
She'd use AI **grudgingly**, checking every word.

steps.text: Choose within a year between law and a hands-on trade
Learn the AI tools the partners bring in, checking every word
Build two months of savings a little at a time

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, one wage, and nothing in the bank. What would help is the government paying people to retrain properly, with a wage while you do it, so someone like me could do an apprenticeship without losing the flat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much of this is about being scared of change, not just about the jobs. I'm not good with new things. I'd want someone to be patient with people like me.

headlineQuote: I'm not good with new things. I'd want someone to be patient with people like me.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old** conveyancing lawyer at a small-town firm, handling about **forty** home sales.
Her bonus depends on completions, she has **nothing saved**, and her partner is an electrician.
She has avoided new software for years and **never uses AI**, preferring careful over quick.
From Steady Disruption on she expects conveyancing to go first; AGI by 2028 leaves her **panicked**.
With more warning she'd consider an **electrical apprenticeship**, since hands-on work lasts longer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: two years, one wage and **nothing** in the bank.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with a wage, so she could do an apprenticeship without losing the flat.
